query: GPU cloud provider raises or cuts GPU rental prices per hour

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Halve to $3.43/Hr in 2026
highlights:
Renting an Nvidia H100 for an hour costs anywhere from $1.30 an hour to as much as $12.29 in October 2026 according to Coloprice, depending on who you ask and which cloud you pick, with GPUFinder naming Lium as the cheapest confirmed H100 at $1.79 an hour and GPU marketplace tracker Uvik putting the median H100 SXM on-demand price at $4.20 across 16 surveyed providers on October 7. That spread, once a rounding error in a niche market, has become one of the clearest signals of how tight the AI compute supply chain still is, two years after ChatGPT turned GPU capacity into a boardroom talking point. Pricing trackers, bank analysts, and Nvidia’s own executives are now telling three overlapping stories at once: H100 rental costs have fallen by roughly half since early 2024, newer chips like the H200 and B200 command a steep premium, and the entire market remains bottlenecked by memory, not by silicon.

...

Pricing tracker Thunder Compute, in a blog post on H100 pricing dated September 1, 2026, lists on-demand H100 80GB rates spanning from $2.89 an hour on RunPod up to $10.98 an hour on Google Cloud’s a3-highgpu-8g instances. CloudZero’s own H100 cost breakdown, published in late August 2026, puts the low end at Vast.ai for as little as $1.49 an hour, though GPUFinder’s October 2026 listing of $1.29 an hour on Hyperbolic now sets the floor, while Rank.ai listed Azure H100 capacity at $6.98 to $12.29 per GPU-hour in October 2026, which stretches the spread at the top even wider. Between those two data points sits a real number that infrastructure teams have to budget against every quarter.

...

Three tiers have emerged in the market and they behave almost like separate products. Marketplace and community-cloud rates sit at the floor, where platforms like RunPod’s community tier and Vast.ai’s peer-to-peer listings undercut everyone else. Specialist clouds such as Lambda, Nebius, and Crusoe occupy the middle, offering more reliability and support without hyperscaler markup (Hyperstack was reported at $2.50 an hour for H100 on a rate checked October 31, 2026, and Modal at $3.9492 an hour on a rate checked October 26, 2026), though that tier is not static: Nebius reportedly increased its H100 price from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour effective October 1, 2026, a rise of about 16.9% that formed part of a rate-card increase of as much as 21%. Hyperscaler on-demand pricing from AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud sits at the top, often two to four times the marketplace floor for the exact same chip.

| Chip | Marketplace / community floor | Specialist cloud (mid-tier) | Hyperscaler on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 80GB | $1.49–$2.99/hr | $3.19–$4.59/hr | $6.88–$10.98/hr |
| H200 141GB | $3.59/hr (RunPod Community) | $4.31–$4.59/hr | $5.58–$6.35/hr |
| B200 | Limited public data | $5.89/hr (RunPod tier cited by Hackceleration) | $8.64/hr (normalized Flex estimate) |

...

Retail-style pricing trackers show a wider range. Lambda lists B200 at $6.69 per GPU-hour for an eight-GPU configuration, RunPod Secure Cloud at $7.99 and Hyperstack at $6.00, while Nebius reportedly charges $8.50 from October 1, 2026 (up from $7.15, an increase of approximately 18.9%), a provider-specific increase rather than a rate every B200 provider charges, CoreWeave’s eight-GPU HGX B200 instance works out to about $8.60 per GPU, and AWS sits at the top of the range at $14.24. A Nebius preemptible B200 listing was reported at $5.00 per GPU-hour in one region on October 29, 2026, though that figure is not directly comparable with on-demand pricing. Blackwell Ultra is priced publicly too: Nebius lists B300 at $9.50 from October 1, 2026, Verda at $8.20, Scaleway at $7.50 and Together AI at $9.99.

...

AIMultiple’s Cloud GPU Rental Price Index, updated August 25, 2026, found that the median H100 rental price across its tracked cohort now sits around $3.38 an hour, down from more than $7 an hour in early 2024. That is a genuine price collapse of over half in just two and a half years, and it reflects the normal pattern for an aging chip: more supply comes online, more providers compete for the same customers, and rates fall. A separate tracker tells a similar story from a slightly later vantage point: the Mercatus GPU Index, measured September 13, 2026, put the average H100 rate at $3.84 an hour across 27 tracked providers, with Lambda listing $3.99 an hour, a reminder that the exact figure depends heavily on which cohort and which averaging method a tracker uses. The GPU Rental Price Index at gpurentalprices.com, which read prices from 1 November 2026 to 6 November 2026, has H100 averaging $3.43 an hour for the month to date, a figure that sits between the AIMultiple and Mercatus readings.

...

Hyperscalers absorb the least pain here. AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud can spread memory cost increases across enormous customer bases and long-term reserved-instance contracts, which is why their on-demand list prices move slower than marketplace spot rates. Specialist clouds like CoreWeave and Nebius sit in the middle, benefiting from the pricing dynamics that Bank of America flagged in an August 17, 2026 note covered by Seeking Alpha, which found both companies “taking advantage of stronger pricing dynamics” as demand for reliable, mid-tier capacity holds up.

## GPU Pricing: What Does AI Compute Actually Cost?

An hourly rate alone hides the real decision. Label every price by billing model — on-demand, spot, reserved, or marketplace/Community Cloud are not the same number, and mixing them produces a false comparison. The table below extends each provider's lowest confirmed on-demand single-GPU H100 rate to 100 hours, 1,000 hours, and 730 hours (roughly one month of continuous use), so the spread is visible at a scale that matches an actual budget rather than a single hour.

📍 In One Sentence

At 730 hours (roughly one month of continuous use), on-demand H100 cost ranges from about $2,110 on RunPod to about $8,970 on Microsoft Azure — a spread of more than 4x driven entirely by provider choice.

💬 In Plain Terms

A single hourly number hides how the cost compounds — the same way a "$5/day" subscription sounds trivial until you see the $1,825/year total. Extending the rate to a realistic usage window is what actually informs a budget decision.

| Provider | Per hour | Per 100 hrs | Per 1,000 hrs | Per 730 hrs (~1 mo) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RunPod (Secure Cloud) | $2.89 | $289 | $2,890 | $2,110 |
| DigitalOcean | $4.41 | $441 | $4,410 | $3,219 |
| Lambda | $3.29 → $3.79 (2026-11-16) | $329 | $3,290 | $2,402 |
| CoreWeave | $6.16 | $616 | $6,160 | $4,497 |
| AWS | $6.88 | $688 | $6,880 | $5,022 |

| Google Cloud | $11.06 | $1,106 | $11,060 | $8,074 |
| Microsoft Azure | $12.29 | $1,229 | $12,290 | $8,972 |

...

GPU Droplets price an H100 at $4.41/GPU-hr on-demand (1 or 8 GPUs per Droplet), with a 12-month reserved rate of $3.26/GPU-hr that requires contacting sales. Billing is per-second with a 5-minute minimum, and a powered-off Droplet is still billed until you destroy it. Deployment is a standard Droplet console — no IAM/VPC configuration overhead before a first workload runs. H100 Droplets include 15,000 GiB of outbound transfer; the pricing page lists no overage rate. The same Droplets serve inference and fine-tuning without a separate product tier, and DigitalOcean also lists H200 ($4.47), AMD MI300X ($2.59) and L40S ($1.57) GPU Droplets per GPU-hour. Its managed-AI catalog is narrower than AWS's and it has no TPUs, so check fit before committing large training runs. Source: DigitalOcean GPU Droplet pricing, checked 2026-11-07; prices change.

...

Lambda is a GPU-first platform built around preconfigured ML environments for researchers and training workloads — and it is no longer just a small GPU-rental company. Lambda listed H100 at $3.29/hr (PCIe) to $4.29/hr (SXM) and A100 at $1.99/hr (40GB) to $2.79/hr (80GB) when last confirmed on 2026-09-05, and its pricing page announces new rates from 2026-11-16 (H100 PCIe $3.79/hr, H100 SXM $4.59-4.89/hr depending on GPU count, A100 40GB $1.99/hr, A100 80GB $3.19/hr in 8-GPU configurations; current rates show only after login); like CoreWeave, its SXM instances are sold only in 8-GPU configurations, so a 2-4 GPU need still pays for all 8. Lambda charges zero egress fees. The platform is built for research and training first: preinstalled ML frameworks, multi-GPU clusters, and support oriented toward serious training runs rather than casual experimentation. Reuters reported on 2026-08-31, citing a source familiar with the matter, that Anthropic signed a cloud-computing deal with Lambda worth a reported $35 billion (not publicly confirmed by the companies), tied to Nvidia GPU capacity coming online via a Hut 8 data-center project in Nueces County covering roughly 350 megawatts — the exact GPU count, contract term, and how obligations split between Anthropic, Lambda, Nvidia, and Hut 8 were not disclosed in the reporting. That scale is the clearest signal that GPU-specialist clouds now compete for serious production workloads, not just researcher side projects.

results.title: H100 Rentals Crashed 70%. Should You Still Buy the GPU? | bex.co
highlights:
Two years ago, renting a single Nvidia H100 cost roughly $8 to $10 per GPU-hour. Today you can get one for about $2.50. That is a 70% price collapse on the most important chip in AI infrastructure, and it quietly rewrote one of the standard arguments in platform engineering: at $8 an hour, buying your own GPU was obviously smart. At $2.50, the answer is genuinely unclear — and the breakeven point moved from “run it a quarter of the time” to “run it nearly around the clock.”

...

| Period | Typical H100 rental (per GPU-hour) | What was happening |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Late 2023 | $7–10, spiking above $12 on major clouds | Acute shortage; hyperscaler-only supply |
| Q4 2024 | $8–10 | Peak scarcity pricing |
| Q1 2025 | $5.50–7.00 | Supply improves as datacenter buildouts land |
| Q2 2025 | $3.50–4.50 | Neocloud capacity floods in |
| Late 2025 | $2.85–3.50 | Market stabilizes at a third of peak |
| 2026 | ~$2–3 on specialized clouds | Median on-demand about $2.99 |

Today's spread tells its own story. Budget marketplaces list H100s from around $1.49 (Vast.ai) to $1.99 (RunPod); managed specialists like Lambda sit near $2.49–3.99; CoreWeave is around $4.25; hyperscalers still charge up to $6.88–6.98 per GPU-hour. The Financial Times noted smaller-provider H100 rates falling roughly another 22% year to date, and AWS itself cut P5 H100 prices 44% back in June 2025. The direction has been down for two straight years.

...

First, the crash is concentrated in on-demand rental on specialized clouds and marketplaces. Hyperscaler on-demand barely budged in comparison: AWS and Azure still charge roughly $7 per H100-hour, nearly triple the neocloud rate. If your workloads live inside a hyperscaler VPC with no exit plan, you have not experienced a 70% price cut. The glut pooled where new capacity was actually built — the neoclouds — and hyperscaler pricing lagged it by the usual 6–12 months, if it follows at all.

results.title: H100 Rental Rates: Why the Hourly Number Isn't the Real Cost
highlights:
Renting an H100 by the hour in 2026 typically costs anywhere from roughly 1.50 to 5 dollars or more per GPU-hour, with the wide spread driven by provider type, commitment length, and region rather than the hardware itself. Specialized neocloud and GPU marketplace providers running spot or short-term on-demand instances tend to sit at the low end of that range, while major hyperscalers charge more for on-demand H100 instances in exchange for broader compliance certifications, integrated services, and enterprise support. Reserved capacity, multi-month commitments, and off-peak or interruptible instances can cut the effective rate substantially compared with on-demand pricing, sometimes by half or more. Multi-GPU instances, such as 8x H100 nodes with InfiniBand, generally carry a modest per-GPU premium over single-GPU instances because of the added networking and NVSwitch hardware. Because rental rates move with GPU supply and newer generations like H200 and Blackwell entering the market, any specific figure should be verified against current provider pricing pages rather than assumed. Nanobase AI advises clients on whether renting or owning H100 capacity makes more sense based on projected utilization and workload duration.

...

A provider's on-demand H100 hourly rate is the easiest number to find and the least useful one for budgeting, because almost no production workload actually pays the on-demand rate for every hour it runs. The number that matters for budgeting is the effective hourly rate after accounting for commitment tier and actual utilization, which can differ from the headline on-demand rate by a wide margin. Skipping

...

| Commitment type | Typical use case | Effect on effective rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On-demand | Short bursts, unpredictable load, evaluation | Highest per-hour rate, no commitment risk |
| Reserved / committed-use | Steady, predictable production traffic | Meaningfully lower rate in exchange for a term commitment |
| Spot / interruptible | Fault-tolerant batch jobs, training checkpoints | Lowest rate, but capacity can be reclaimed with little notice |
| Multi-GPU node (8x H100 + InfiniBand) | Distributed training, tensor-parallel inference | Modest per-GPU premium over single-GPU instances |

...

The effective hourly cost a workload actually pays is a function of the quoted rate, the commitment discount, and the share of hours the GPU sits idle:

1. Start with the on-demand rate for the target GPU and instance size.
2. Apply the commitment discount if reserving capacity; reserved and multi-month terms have historically cut effective rates by roughly half or more relative to on-demand.
3. Divide the workload's actual running hours by total hours in the billing period to get the utilization fraction, since reserved capacity is paid for whether it is busy or idle.
4. Effective cost per useful hour = (committed rate x total hours billed) / (hours the GPU was actually doing useful work).
5. Compare that effective cost per useful hour across commitment tiers and providers, not the headline on-demand rate alone.
